question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Justice KS Puttaswamy regarding the right to privacy under Article 21?
key_legal_points: Right to privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21
Privacy is an intrinsic part of life and personal liberty
State intrusions must satisfy legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality
ground_truth_answer: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a 9-judge bench of the Supreme Court unanimously held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution.

question: What is the basic structure doctrine established in Kesavananda Bharati?
key_legal_points: Parliament has wide amending power under Article 368
Amending power cannot alter or destroy the basic structure or essential framework
Judicial review, secularism, democracy and rule of law are basic structure elements
ground_truth_answer: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) held by a 7:6 majority that while Parliament has extensive constituent power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, it cannot alter or destroy the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution.

question: How did Maneka Gandhi expand the interpretation of personal liberty and procedure established by law?
key_legal_points: Procedure depriving personal liberty must be just, fair and reasonable
Articles 14, 19, and 21 form an interconnected golden triangle
Overruled narrow interpretation from AK Gopalan
ground_truth_answer: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) established that 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 cannot be arbitrary or oppressive; it must be just, fair, and reasonable, incorporating substantive due process and uniting Articles 14, 19, and 21.

question: What remedies are provided under Article 32 for the enforcement of fundamental rights?
key_legal_points: Right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Part III rights is itself a fundamental right
Supreme Court has power to issue writs including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari
ground_truth_answer: Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of Part III fundamental rights, empowering the Court to issue directions, orders, or prerogative writs.

question: What did Minerva Mills hold regarding the balance between fundamental rights and directive principles?
key_legal_points: Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Part III and Part IV
Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 seeking to exclude judicial review were held unconstitutional
ground_truth_answer: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) held that the Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part IV (Directive Principles). To give absolute primacy to one over the other destroys the harmony of the Constitution.

question: What principles on secularism and state government dismissal were laid down in SR Bommai?
key_legal_points: Secularism is an integral component of the basic structure
Proclamation of President Rule under Article 356 is subject to judicial review
Floor test is the mandatory method to test executive majority
ground_truth_answer: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) affirmed that secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution and held that presidential proclamations under Article 356 are subject to judicial review, requiring floor tests on the assembly floor.

question: What six fundamental freedoms are guaranteed to Indian citizens under Article 19?
key_legal_points: Freedom of speech and expression
Freedom to assemble peaceably without arms
Freedom to form associations or unions
Freedom of movement across India
Freedom to reside and settle anywhere in India
Freedom to practise any profession, trade or business
ground_truth_answer: Article 19 guarantees six basic freedoms to citizens subject to reasonable restrictions under clauses (2) to (6).

question: How is equality before law and equal protection of laws defined under Article 14?
key_legal_points: State shall not deny equality before law
Equal protection of laws within territory of India
Applies to citizens and non-citizens alike
ground_truth_answer: Article 14 ensures that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or equal protection of the laws within India.

question: What is the definition of the term State under Article 12 of the Constitution?
key_legal_points: Government and Parliament of India
Government and Legislature of States
All local or other authorities within India or under Government control
ground_truth_answer: Article 12 defines State to include the Union Government, Parliament, State Governments, State Legislatures, and local or other authorities.

question: What does Article 21A provide regarding the fundamental right to free education?
key_legal_points: Free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14
Inserted by 86th Constitutional Amendment 2002
ground_truth_answer: Article 21A mandates that the State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years.

question: What protections exist against retrospective criminal laws under Article 20(1)?
key_legal_points: No person convicted except for violation of law in force at commission
No greater penalty than that prescribed at commission time
ground_truth_answer: Article 20(1) prohibits ex-post facto criminal laws, ensuring no person is convicted or penalized under laws enacted after the act.

question: Explain the prohibition of double jeopardy under Article 20(2)
key_legal_points: No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once
ground_truth_answer: Article 20(2) guarantees that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.

question: What is the protection against self-incrimination guaranteed in Article 20(3)?
key_legal_points: No person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself
ground_truth_answer: Article 20(3) states that no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.

question: What safeguards against arrest and detention are provided in Article 22?
key_legal_points: Right to be informed of grounds of arrest
Right to consult legal practitioner
Right to be produced before magistrate within 24 hours
ground_truth_answer: Article 22 mandates informing arrested individuals of grounds, legal representation, and magistrate production within 24 hours.

question: What prohibition does Article 23 impose on human trafficking and begar?
key_legal_points: Traffic in human beings and begar are prohibited
Any contravention is an offence punishable by law
ground_truth_answer: Article 23 prohibits human trafficking, begar, and other forced labour forms, making violations criminally punishable.

question: What is the constitutional age limit for hazardous child employment under Article 24?
key_legal_points: No child below age fourteen years shall be employed in factories or hazardous work
ground_truth_answer: Article 24 strictly prohibits employing children below the age of fourteen years in factories, mines, or hazardous occupations.

question: What freedom of religion is guaranteed to all persons under Article 25?
key_legal_points: Freedom of conscience and right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion
Subject to public order, morality and health
ground_truth_answer: Article 25 grants all persons freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise, and propagate religion subject to public order, morality, and health.

question: What rights do religious denominations possess under Article 26?
key_legal_points: Establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes
Manage their own affairs in matters of religion
Own and acquire movable and immovable property
ground_truth_answer: Article 26 guarantees religious denominations rights to establish institutions, manage religious affairs, and own property.

question: Explain freedom from taxation for religious promotion under Article 27
key_legal_points: No person compelled to pay taxes proceeds of which are appropriated for promoting any religion
ground_truth_answer: Article 27 prohibits the State from compelling citizens to pay taxes dedicated to promoting or maintaining any specific religion.

question: What does Article 28 provide regarding religious instruction in State-funded schools?
key_legal_points: No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
Voluntary attendance in State-aided schools
ground_truth_answer: Article 28 bars religious instruction in schools wholly maintained by State funds and requires consent in State-aided institutions.

question: How are minority languages and scripts protected under Article 29?
key_legal_points: Any section of citizens with distinct language, script or culture has right to conserve it
No denial of admission to State-aided institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste, language
ground_truth_answer: Article 29 protects cultural and linguistic conservation rights and prohibits discriminatory admission to State-aided educational institutions.

question: What rights do minorities have to administer educational institutions under Article 30?
key_legal_points: All minorities based on religion or language have right to establish and administer educational institutions
ground_truth_answer: Article 30 guarantees religious and linguistic minorities the fundamental right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

question: What is the constitutional effect of Article 13 on laws violating fundamental rights?
key_legal_points: All laws in force inconsistent with Part III are void to the extent of inconsistency
State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges Part III rights
ground_truth_answer: Article 13 declares that laws in force inconsistent with Part III are void, and prohibits enactments abridging fundamental rights.

question: What directive does Article 39A give regarding free legal aid?
key_legal_points: State shall ensure legal system promotes justice on basis of equal opportunity
Provide free legal aid through suitable legislation or schemes
ground_truth_answer: Article 39A mandates the State to secure equal justice and provide free legal aid to ensure justice is not denied by economic disability.

question: What is the constitutional directive on village panchayats in Article 40?
key_legal_points: State shall organize village panchayats and endow them with powers as units of self-government
ground_truth_answer: Article 40 directs the State to organize village panchayats and endow them with powers necessary to function as self-governing units.

question: What does Article 44 say about a Uniform Civil Code?
key_legal_points: State shall endeavour to secure for citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India
ground_truth_answer: Article 44 directs the State to endeavour to secure for all citizens a Uniform Civil Code across India.

question: What environmental directive is contained in Article 48A?
key_legal_points: State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife
ground_truth_answer: Article 48A directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.

question: What separation is mandated by Article 50 of the Constitution?
key_legal_points: State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services
ground_truth_answer: Article 50 directs the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services.

question: What fundamental duties are prescribed under Article 51A?
key_legal_points: Abide by Constitution and respect Flag and Anthem
Cherish ideals of freedom struggle
Uphold sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India
Promote harmony and renounce practices derogatory to dignity of women
ground_truth_answer: Article 51A enumerates eleven fundamental duties of citizens, including respecting the Constitution, defending the nation, and protecting the environment.

question: What is the executive power of the President of India under Article 53?
key_legal_points: Executive power of Union vested in President
Exercised directly or through officers subordinate
Supreme command of Defence Forces
ground_truth_answer: Article 53 vests executive power of the Union and supreme command of the armed forces in the President of India.

question: What pardoning powers does the President have under Article 72?
key_legal_points: Power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment
Applies to court-martial sentences, Union law offences, and death sentences
ground_truth_answer: Article 72 empowers the President to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment in offences against Union law or death penalties.

question: What is the role of the Council of Ministers under Article 74?
key_legal_points: Council of Ministers with Prime Minister at head to aid and advise President
President shall act in accordance with advice after reconsideration if sought
ground_truth_answer: Article 74 establishes the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President in exercising executive functions.

question: What is the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131?
key_legal_points: Exclusive original jurisdiction in legal disputes between Government of India and States or between States
ground_truth_answer: Article 131 gives the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction in disputes involving legal rights between the Union and States or between States.

question: What is Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136?
key_legal_points: Discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, sentence or order in India
ground_truth_answer: Article 136 grants the Supreme Court plenary discretion to grant special leave to appeal from any court or tribunal in India.

question: What binding effect does Supreme Court law have under Article 141?
key_legal_points: Law declared by Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India
ground_truth_answer: Article 141 provides that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within India.

question: What plenary power does Article 142 confer on the Supreme Court?
key_legal_points: Power to pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter
ground_truth_answer: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass orders necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter before it.

question: Explain the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 143
key_legal_points: President may refer questions of law or fact of public importance to Supreme Court for opinion
ground_truth_answer: Article 143 authorizes the President to consult the Supreme Court on questions of law or fact of public importance.

question: What writ powers do High Courts exercise under Article 226?
key_legal_points: Power to issue directions, orders or writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose
ground_truth_answer: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs not only for fundamental rights enforcement but also for 'any other purpose'.

question: What power of superintendence does Article 227 give High Courts?
key_legal_points: Superintendence over all courts and tribunals throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction
ground_truth_answer: Article 227 gives High Courts administrative and judicial superintendence over all subordinate courts and tribunals within their jurisdiction.

question: How does Article 254 resolve conflicts between Union and State laws?
key_legal_points: Union law prevails over inconsistent State law on Concurrent List matters unless President assented
ground_truth_answer: Article 254 establishes Union legislative supremacy in Concurrent List matters, voiding repugnant State laws unless presidential assent was obtained.

question: What does Article 300A guarantee regarding property rights?
key_legal_points: No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law
ground_truth_answer: Article 300A guarantees that no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law, making it a constitutional right.

question: What safeguards are given to civil servants under Article 311?
key_legal_points: No dismissal by authority subordinate to appointing authority
Reasonable opportunity of being heard in inquiry
ground_truth_answer: Article 311 shields civil servants from dismissal by subordinate authorities and guarantees a reasonable opportunity of being heard in disciplinary inquiries.

question: What powers does Article 324 vest in the Election Commission?
key_legal_points: Superintendence, direction and control of preparation of electoral rolls and conduct of elections
ground_truth_answer: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction, and control of parliamentary, state, presidential, and vice-presidential elections in the Election Commission.

question: What are the grounds for declaring National Emergency under Article 352?
key_legal_points: War, external aggression, or armed rebellion threatening security of India or any territory
ground_truth_answer: Article 352 permits national emergency declarations if the security of India is threatened by war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.

question: What grounds justify President Rule under Article 356?
key_legal_points: Failure of constitutional machinery in State where governance cannot be carried on in accordance with Constitution
ground_truth_answer: Article 356 enables the President to assume State governance upon satisfaction that constitutional governance has broken down in that State.

question: What did the 42nd Amendment 1976 add to the Preamble?
key_legal_points: Added the words 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' to the Preamble
ground_truth_answer: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976 amended the Preamble to insert the words 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity'.

question: What changes did the 44th Amendment 1978 make to Article 359 emergency powers?
key_legal_points: Prohibited suspension of enforcement of Article 20 and Article 21 during emergencies
Replaced internal disturbance with armed rebellion
ground_truth_answer: The 44th Amendment Act 1978 ensured that the right to enforce Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during an emergency proclamation.

question: What voting age change was made by the 61st Amendment Act 1988?
key_legal_points: Lowered the voting age for Lok Sabha and Assembly elections from 21 years to 18 years under Article 326
ground_truth_answer: The 61st Amendment Act 1988 amended Article 326 to lower the voting age from 21 years to 18 years for parliamentary and state assembly elections.

question: What local governance system did the 73rd Amendment establish?
key_legal_points: Three-tier Panchayati Raj system with constitutional status, regular elections, and 33 percent women reservation
ground_truth_answer: The 73rd Amendment Act 1992 created Part IX of the Constitution, giving constitutional backing to three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions.

question: What reservation was introduced by the 103rd Amendment Act 2019?
key_legal_points: Up to 10 percent reservation for Economically Weaker Sections EWS in admissions and public employment
ground_truth_answer: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act 2019 inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6) providing up to 10 percent reservation for Economically Weaker Sections.

question: What did the Supreme Court hold in Shankari Prasad 1951 regarding amending power?
key_legal_points: Constitutional amendments under Article 368 are not 'law' under Article 13(2)
Parliament can amend fundamental rights
ground_truth_answer: Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951) held that constitutional amendments under Article 368 are exercises of constituent power and do not constitute 'law' under Article 13(2).

question: What did Golak Nath 1967 hold regarding fundamental rights amendment?
key_legal_points: Fundamental rights occupy a transcendental position
Parliament has no power to abridge or take away Part III rights by amendment
ground_truth_answer: I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967) held by 6:5 majority that fundamental rights cannot be curtailed by constitutional amendments under Article 368.

question: How did Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain apply the basic structure doctrine?
key_legal_points: Struck down Article 329A(4) 39th Amendment which validated prime minister election without judicial review
ground_truth_answer: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) applied the basic structure doctrine to strike down Article 329A(4), holding free elections and judicial review as basic features.

question: What did Waman Rao establish regarding Ninth Schedule laws?
key_legal_points: Laws added to Ninth Schedule prior to 24 April 1973 Kesavananda date are valid
Post-1973 laws subject to basic structure review
ground_truth_answer: Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) drew a cutoff line on 24 April 1973: Ninth Schedule laws enacted before Kesavananda are immune, while later enactments are reviewable.

question: What did IR Coelho 2007 hold on judicial review of Ninth Schedule laws?
key_legal_points: All laws inserted into Ninth Schedule post-Kesavananda must satisfy basic structure and fundamental rights tests
ground_truth_answer: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) confirmed unanimously that post-1973 Ninth Schedule enactments can be invalidated if they damage basic structure principles.

question: What narrow interpretation was laid down in AK Gopalan 1950?
key_legal_points: Article 21 procedure established by law means state-enacted statutory procedure without natural justice review
Articles 19 and 21 are mutually exclusive
ground_truth_answer: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) held that 'procedure established by law' simply meant procedure prescribed by statute, rejecting natural justice integration into Article 21.

question: What did Sunil Batra hold regarding solitary confinement and prisoner rights?
key_legal_points: Prisoners retain fundamental rights
Solitary confinement and bar fetters without judicial order violate Article 21
ground_truth_answer: Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration (1978) established that prisoners retain enforceable fundamental rights under Article 21 against cruel, inhuman punishment.

question: What did Olga Tellis hold regarding pavement dwellers and livelihood under Article 21?
key_legal_points: Right to life includes right to livelihood
Evictions must follow natural justice and procedural fairness
ground_truth_answer: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) held that the right to livelihood is an essential facet of the right to life under Article 21.

question: What did Francis Coralie Mullin hold regarding human dignity under Article 21?
key_legal_points: Right to life means more than animal existence; includes right to live with human dignity
ground_truth_answer: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi (1981) ruled that Article 21 guarantees life with human dignity and basic necessities.

question: What did EP Royappa establish regarding the concept of equality under Article 14?
key_legal_points: Equality is a dynamic concept antithetical to arbitrariness
Arbitrary action by State violates Article 14
ground_truth_answer: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) formulated the non-arbitrariness doctrine: equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies; an arbitrary act violates Article 14.

question: What did Indra Sawhney hold regarding the 50 percent reservation limit and creamy layer?
key_legal_points: Upheld 27 percent OBC quota
Reservations should not exceed 50 percent except in extraordinary circumstances
Creamy layer must be excluded from backward classes
ground_truth_answer: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) upheld 27 percent OBC reservations, established the 50 percent ceiling rule, and mandated creamy layer exclusion.

question: What did M Nagaraj hold regarding reservation in promotions for SC and ST?
key_legal_points: Upheld constitutional amendments enabling reservations in promotion
State must show quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequate representation, and administrative efficiency
ground_truth_answer: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) upheld enabling promotion amendments subject to State demonstrating quantifiable backwardness and administrative efficiency data.

question: What did Romesh Thappar establish regarding pre-censorship of the press?
key_legal_points: Freedom of speech includes freedom of circulation
Pre-censorship or ban on circulation violates Article 19(1)(a)
ground_truth_answer: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950) held that freedom of speech includes freedom of circulation, striking down executive entry bans on periodicals.

question: What did Bennett Coleman hold on newsprint import restrictions?
key_legal_points: Newsprint policy directly controlled newspaper page limits and circulation
Violated freedom of the press under Article 19(1)(a)
ground_truth_answer: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1972) held that government newsprint quotas fixing maximum pages curtailed newspaper circulation and violated Article 19(1)(a).

question: What did Shreya Singhal hold regarding Section 66A of the IT Act?
key_legal_points: Struck down Section 66A IT Act for vagueness and overbreadth
Chilling effect on legitimate online speech violating Article 19(1)(a)
ground_truth_answer: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act for being unconstitutionally vague and overbroad.

question: What did Anuradha Bhasin decide on indefinite internet shutdowns?
key_legal_points: Freedom of speech and profession over internet is protected under Article 19
Indefinite internet shutdowns violate proportionality; orders must be published and periodically reviewed
ground_truth_answer: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) held that internet speech and trade are constitutionally protected, and indefinite shutdowns violate proportionality standards.

question: What is the essential religious practices test established in Shirur Mutt?
key_legal_points: Protection under Articles 25 and 26 extends only to practices essential to a religion as determined by its tenets
ground_truth_answer: Commissioner, HRE Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar (Shirur Mutt, 1954) established that constitutional protection extends to essential religious practices.

question: What did Shayara Bano hold regarding instant triple talaq?
key_legal_points: Talaq-e-biddat instant triple talaq is arbitrary and unconstitutional under Article 14
ground_truth_answer: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) struck down instant triple talaq by 3:2 majority as manifestly arbitrary and violative of Article 14.

question: What did Indian Young Lawyers Association decide in Sabarimala 2018?
key_legal_points: Exclusion of women of menstruating age violated equality under Article 14 and religious freedom under Article 25
ground_truth_answer: Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018) held that excluding women aged 10-50 from Sabarimala violated constitutional morality and Article 14.

question: What did Bijoe Emmanuel decide regarding singing the National Anthem?
key_legal_points: Respectfully standing without singing due to religious beliefs protected under Article 19(1)(a) and Article 25
ground_truth_answer: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) protected students expelled for standing respectfully without singing the anthem on sincere religious conscience grounds.

question: What did the Second Judges Case establish regarding judicial appointments?
key_legal_points: Consultation means concurrence of Chief Justice of India
Created the collegium system of judicial appointments
ground_truth_answer: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (1993) established that 'consultation' implies concurrence, creating the collegium appointment system.

question: Why did the Fourth Judges Case 2015 invalidate the NJAC Act?
key_legal_points: Judicial primacy in appointments is part of independence of judiciary and basic structure
NJAC gave executive veto power compromising independence
ground_truth_answer: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) struck down the 99th Amendment and NJAC as unconstitutional infringements on judicial independence.

question: What did the dissenting judgment of Justice HR Khanna in ADM Jabalpur state?
key_legal_points: Article 21 is not the sole repository of right to life and personal liberty
Rule of law cannot be suspended even during presidential emergency proclamations
ground_truth_answer: Justice H.R. Khanna famously dissented in ADM Jabalpur (1976), stating that the state has no power to deprive people of life without law, even in emergencies.

question: What arrest guidelines did the Supreme Court lay down in DK Basu 1997?
key_legal_points: Mandatory 11 guidelines including memo of arrest, notifying family, medical examination every 48 hours
ground_truth_answer: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) formulated mandatory guidelines for arrest, detention, and interrogation to eliminate custodial torture.

question: What did Vishaka v State of Rajasthan establish regarding workplace sexual harassment?
key_legal_points: Formulated binding Vishaka guidelines under Article 141 and Article 32 incorporating CEDAW international convention
ground_truth_answer: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) laid down legally binding workplace sexual harassment guidelines to fill statutory vacuum until legislative enactments.

question: What did Navtej Singh Johar decide regarding Section 377 IPC?
key_legal_points: Decriminalized consensual adult same-sex acts under Section 377 as violative of equality, privacy, and dignity
ground_truth_answer: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) unanimously read down Section 377 IPC, holding that criminalizing consensual adult relationships violates Articles 14 and 21.

question: What did Joseph Shine 2018 decide on the crime of adultery under Section 497?
key_legal_points: Section 497 treated married women as husband property, violating gender equality and personal dignity under Articles 14 and 21
ground_truth_answer: Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) unanimously struck down Section 497 of the IPC, holding the penal offense of adultery manifestly arbitrary and discriminatory.

question: What did Common Cause 2018 decide on living wills and passive euthanasia?
key_legal_points: Right to die with dignity is an inseparable facet of Article 21
Sanctioned advance medical directives living wills
ground_truth_answer: Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) recognized the right to die with dignity, legalizing passive euthanasia and advance medical directives.

question: What did Selvi v State of Karnataka hold regarding involuntary narco-analysis?
key_legal_points: Involuntary administration of polygraph, narco-analysis, and brain mapping violates Article 20(3) and privacy under Article 21
ground_truth_answer: Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) held that involuntary narco-analysis and lie-detector tests violate the protection against self-incrimination and mental privacy.

question: What did Lily Thomas 2013 hold regarding disqualification of convicted lawmakers?
key_legal_points: Struck down Section 8(4) RPA which permitted convicted legislators to remain in office pending appeals
ground_truth_answer: Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013) struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, ruling that convicted MPs and MLAs stand disqualified immediately.

question: What did ADR 2002 hold regarding voter rights to candidate information?
key_legal_points: Voters have fundamental right to know candidate criminal records, assets, and education under Article 19(1)(a)
ground_truth_answer: Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) ruled that voters have a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) to know candidates' backgrounds.

question: What did Kihoto Hollohan 1992 hold on Speaker decisions under the Tenth Schedule?
key_legal_points: Speaker acts as a tribunal when deciding disqualification and is subject to judicial review under Articles 136 and 226
ground_truth_answer: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) upheld the Tenth Schedule but held that Speaker disqualification orders act as tribunal decisions subject to judicial review.
